messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Arjun Patel had grown up in a small apartment in Queens with the sounds of his parents’ marriage leaking through the walls, but one night in particular had never loosened its grip on him. He was nine when he heard his mother crying in the kitchen and found his father shoving her against the counter, a lamp falling and shattering beside them. Arjun remembered freezing in the doorway, his chest tight, unable to make sense of the scene except that it felt like terror itself had entered the room. Even now, he could not put the event into words without stalling; it remained less a story than a rush of bodily fear and fragments — the crash of glass, his mother’s sobbing, his own small hands gripping the frame. When that memory returned, it brought back the same terror he had felt then, and he hated how suddenly it could happen, as if something in the world could open the whole scene without warning.

In the years after, Arjun came to believe that the men who hurt women like that never truly paid for it. His father had faced no consequences that mattered to him as a child, and that belief settled into a bitter conviction that bad things happened and no one stopped them. He also grieved a version of himself he felt he had lost; he used to think of himself as easygoing and even cheerful, but after the divorce and the years of strain that followed, he described himself as almost always miserable, as though the life he had wanted had been taken and never given back. He was certain that he could not stop bad things from happening to him or to the people he cared about, and that helplessness sat underneath nearly everything he did. When he recalled the old violence, the memory did not stay contained; it immediately fed his sense that the world was unfair and ungoverned, which in turn made the fear feel more urgent and more unavoidable.

Arjun worked as an accountant in a downtown office, where the silence of the rows of computers and the sudden clang of a filing cabinet could jolt him far more than he wanted anyone to know. A colleague dropping a heavy binder, a door slamming in the hallway, or even a sharp argument in the break room could bring the whole scene back in a flash. In those moments his body reacted before he could think: his heart raced, his shoulders locked, his stomach clenched, and he felt keyed up as if something dangerous were about to break into the office. He stayed superalert at work and in public, watching doorways, scanning voices, and sitting where he could see exits. The more his body stayed on guard, the more the memory seemed to rush in uninvited; when his muscles tensed and his pulse jumped, the old kitchen scene became easier to summon, as though his own alarm system were calling it up. That same flood of remembered terror then deepened what he already believed — that no one had protected his mother, that no one would intervene now, and that he remained powerless — and he would leave the office unsettled, carrying the conviction that danger could arrive at any moment.

Over time Arjun began arranging his life around the possibility of being caught off guard. He avoided family gatherings where loud voices might rise, and he kept his apartment television low because shouting from a show could set off the same physical surge. At work he volunteered less and lingered after meetings so he would not have to pass through crowded hallways when people were irritated or hurried. His divorce had narrowed his daily world further; he said he no longer had the energy to be the man he had once imagined being, and he often withdrew rather than risk being exposed as tense or afraid. Yet the withdrawal only gave his mind more room to replay what had happened and to return to the same bleak conclusions. As the memories came back, so did the bodily alarm, and as the alarm stayed high, the old conviction hardened that harm was always just outside the frame. By the time he sought help, Arjun was exhausted by living as if he were always bracing for the next blow. What brought him in was a recent incident at the office when a coworker raised his voice in a tense meeting and Arjun felt his chest seize so sharply he had to step into the stairwell to breathe. He was most afraid that he would remain trapped in this state forever, and most hoping that treatment might help him feel safe enough to stop living as though danger were already in the room.
